items.stem: Which of the following best describes "utility maximisation"?
options: The model of the economic agent as a fully rational, self-interested utility maximiser
The design of the way choices are presented to people, which influences the decisions they make
A branch of economics that uses insights from psychology to explain why people's decisions often deviate from the rational choice model
The assumption that consumers aim to gain the greatest possible satisfaction from their limited income
items.answer: The assumption that consumers aim to gain the greatest possible satisfaction from their limited income
items.markingKey: D. "utility maximisation" is the assumption that consumers aim to gain the greatest possible satisfaction from their limited income.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "If a consumer buys something they regret later, this proves the rational choice model is useless." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: One mistake does not invalidate a model of average behaviour; however, systematic, predictable errors (e.g. present bias) do challenge its assumptions, which is the focus of behavioural economics.
items.markingKey: One mistake does not invalidate a model of average behaviour; however, systematic, predictable errors (e.g. present bias) do challenge its assumptions, which is the focus of behavioural economics. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between behavioural economics and the rational choice model.
items.answer: Rational choice assumes consistent preferences, perfect information and utility maximisation; behavioural economics uses psychology and evidence to show systematic deviations such as biases and bounded rationality.
items.markingKey: Rational choice assumes consistent preferences, perfect information and utility maximisation; behavioural economics uses psychology and evidence to show systematic deviations such as biases and bounded rationality. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that if a consumer buys something they regret later, this proves the rational choice model is useless. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: One mistake does not invalidate a model of average behaviour; however, systematic, predictable errors (e.g. present bias) do challenge its assumptions, which is the focus of behavioural economics.
items.markingKey: One mistake does not invalidate a model of average behaviour; however, systematic, predictable errors (e.g. present bias) do challenge its assumptions, which is the focus of behavioural economics. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "If a consumer buys something they regret later, this proves the rational choice model is useless." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: One mistake does not invalidate a model of average behaviour; however, systematic, predictable errors (e.g. present bias) do challenge its assumptions, which is the focus of behavioural economics.
items.markingKey: One mistake does not invalidate a model of average behaviour; however, systematic, predictable errors (e.g. present bias) do challenge its assumptions, which is the focus of behavioural economics. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the assumptions of rational consumer choice are so unrealistic that the theory should be abandoned.
items.answer: The theory should be retained as a benchmark but supplemented by behavioural insights where its assumptions fail.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: evidence of biases, limited information and inconsistent preferences; behavioural economics predicts some choices better. Arguments against: rational choice explains much market behaviour, e.g. responses to prices; behavioural economics builds on, rather than replaces, it; simple assumptions make models tractable. Supported judgement: The theory should be retained as a benchmark but supplemented by behavioural insights where its assumptions fail.

items.stem: Define the term "rational consumer choice".
items.answer: The assumption that consumers make choices that maximise their utility, given their preferences, incomes and prices
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the assumption that consumers make choices that maximise their utility, given their preferences, incomes and prices. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why consistent preferences are important for the rational choice model.
items.answer: If preferences changed randomly or were not transitive, consumers' choices could not be predicted and demand curves would not be stable; the model relies on stable preferences to predict behaviour.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If preferences changed randomly or were not transitive, consumers' choices could not be predicted and demand curves would not be stable; the model relies on stable preferences to predict behaviour. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between utility and price.
items.answer: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gains from a good; price is what must be paid for it. A rational consumer compares the two at the margin.
items.markingKey: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gains from a good; price is what must be paid for it. A rational consumer compares the two at the margin. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

A regulator found that 60% of households had not switched energy supplier in the previous three years, even though switching could save an average of £300 a year. Many said comparing tariffs was 'too complicated' or that they 'never got round to it'.
— Extract based on an energy regulator's market review

Using the extract, explain why consumer behaviour may not match the assumptions of rational consumer choice.
items.answer: Rational consumers with perfect information would switch to save £300; complexity (imperfect information, bounded rationality) and inertia (bounded self-control/status quo bias) prevent utility-maximising choices.
items.markingKey: Rational consumers with perfect information would switch to save £300; complexity (imperfect information, bounded rationality) and inertia (bounded self-control/status quo bias) prevent utility-maximising choices. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the large number of mobile phone and energy tariffs in many countries shows the limits of the perfect information assumption.
items.answer: Studies by regulators such as the UK's Ofgem found that many consumers stayed on expensive default tariffs rather than switching. Complex tariffs make full comparison difficult, so consumers do not maximise utility as the rational model predicts.
items.markingKey: Context (Studies by regulators such as the UK's Ofgem found that many consumers stayed on expensive default tariffs rather than switching.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Complex tariffs make full comparison difficult, so consumers do not maximise utility as the rational model predicts. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of the perfect information assumption.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that consumers generally act in their own best interests.
items.answer: Consumers often act in their own interest, but systematic biases and information problems mean they sometimes do not, which justifies some policy responses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: people know their own preferences best; markets respond to consumer choices. Arguments against: biases such as present bias and anchoring cause systematic mistakes; imperfect information and complexity (pensions, insurance); addiction and habits. Judgement: Consumers often act in their own interest, but systematic biases and information problems mean they sometimes do not, which justifies some policy responses. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. Level 4 (10-12) evaluation present but not fully developed. Level 3 (7-9) some evaluation, explanation partly developed. Level 2 (4-6) limited explanation, little evaluation. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: A person buys flood insurance immediately after seeing news of floods in a nearby town. Which bias is this?
items.answer: Availability bias
items.markingKey: A. Recent, vivid examples make the risk seem more likely.

items.stem: Explain how loss aversion can affect consumer choices.
items.answer: People feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains, so they may hold on to things they own (endowment effect) or respond more to a charge than to a bonus of the same size.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: People feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains, so they may hold on to things they own (endowment effect) or respond more to a charge than to a bonus of the same size. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Buying a gym membership and never going is an example of bounded selfishness." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is an example of bounded self-control (and over-optimism): people overestimate their future willpower. Bounded selfishness concerns concern for others.
items.markingKey: It is an example of bounded self-control (and over-optimism): people overestimate their future willpower. Bounded selfishness concerns concern for others. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A restaurant places an expensive $90 dish at the top of its menu, although few people order it. Explain the behavioural reason for this strategy.
items.answer: Anchoring: the expensive item makes other dishes (e.g. $40) seem reasonable by comparison, increasing spending on mid-priced items.
items.markingKey: Anchoring: the expensive item makes other dishes (e.g. $40) seem reasonable by comparison, increasing spending on mid-priced items.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how bounded self-control can lead to overconsumption of a good such as sugary snacks.
items.answer: Diagram: P vs Q; demand reflects the perceived marginal benefit at the moment of purchase (D = MPB perceived), which is higher than the true long-run marginal benefit to the consumer (MB true) because of present bias. The market quantity Q1 exceeds Q* where the true benefit equals cost, so consumers over-consume relative to their own long-run interest.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: P vs Q; demand reflects the perceived marginal benefit at the moment of purchase (D = MPB perceived), which is higher than the true long-run marginal benefit to the consumer (MB true) because of present bias. The market quantity Q1 exceeds Q* where the true benefit equals cost, so consumers over-consume relative to their own long-run interest. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Behavioural economics provides a more accurate explanation of consumer behaviour than traditional rational choice theory."
items.answer: Behavioural economics improves the explanation of many individual decisions, but rational choice remains a useful benchmark for aggregate market behaviour.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: evidence of anchoring, framing, present bias and social norms; explains under-saving, over-eating and inertia; has produced successful policies (auto-enrolment). Arguments against: many findings come from laboratory experiments and may not generalise; rational choice predicts aggregate market responses well; biases vary across people and contexts and some studies fail to replicate. Supported judgement: Behavioural economics improves the explanation of many individual decisions, but rational choice remains a useful benchmark for aggregate market behaviour.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The tendency to judge the likelihood of an event by how easily examples come to mind"?
items.answer: availability bias
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of availability bias.

items.stem: Distinguish between anchoring and framing.
items.answer: Anchoring is relying on an initial number or piece of information as a reference point; framing is being influenced by how the same information is presented (e.g. as a gain or a loss).
items.markingKey: Anchoring is relying on an initial number or piece of information as a reference point; framing is being influenced by how the same information is presented (e.g. as a gain or a loss). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe Herbert Simon's concept of satisficing and explain what it reveals about bounded rationality.
items.answer: Simon (Nobel 1978) argued that decision-makers seek a satisfactory outcome rather than the optimal one because they face limited information and processing capacity. Rather than maximise, consumers and firms stop searching once an acceptable option is found.
items.markingKey: Context (Simon (Nobel 1978) argued that decision-makers seek a satisfactory outcome rather than the optimal one because they face limited information and processing capacity.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rather than maximise, consumers and firms stop searching once an acceptable option is found. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to bounded rationality.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

A charity tested two letters. One said: 'Your gift of $50 will provide clean water to a family for a year.' The other said: 'Millions of people lack clean water.' The first letter raised 60% more money.
— Hypothetical charity trial

Using the extract, explain which behavioural concepts help explain the result.
items.answer: Framing (concrete, identifiable impact) and bounded selfishness (people care about others' welfare); the vivid, specific frame triggers more giving than an abstract statistic (availability/identifiable victim effect).
items.markingKey: Framing (concrete, identifiable impact) and bounded selfishness (people care about others' welfare); the vivid, specific frame triggers more giving than an abstract statistic (availability/identifiable victim effect). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Who wrote the book Nudge (2008)?
items.answer: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein
items.markingKey: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein. Thaler and Sunstein popularised the term nudge and 'libertarian paternalism'.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a nudge and a regulation.
items.answer: A nudge changes how choices are presented while keeping all options open; a regulation forbids or requires behaviour by law.
items.markingKey: A nudge changes how choices are presented while keeping all options open; a regulation forbids or requires behaviour by law. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why nudges are described as 'libertarian paternalism'.
items.answer: They steer people towards choices judged to be in their interest (paternalism) while leaving them free to choose otherwise (libertarian), as no option is banned and incentives are not significantly changed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They steer people towards choices judged to be in their interest (paternalism) while leaving them free to choose otherwise (libertarian), as no option is banned and incentives are not significantly changed. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe England's switch to an opt-out organ donation system in 2020 and explain what it reveals about default choice architecture.
items.answer: Under 'Max and Keira's Law', adults are presumed to be donors unless they opt out, following similar changes in Wales (2015). Changing the default is expected to raise the number of registered donors because most people do not actively opt out.
items.markingKey: Context (Under 'Max and Keira's Law', adults are presumed to be donors unless they opt out, following similar changes in Wales (2015).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Changing the default is expected to raise the number of registered donors because most people do not actively opt out. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to default choice architecture.

items.stem: Explain how a government could use choice architecture to increase the number of people who get a flu vaccination.
items.answer: e.g. send letters with a pre-booked appointment time (default), reminders by text, or make the vaccination point easy to reach; this uses inertia and salience rather than incentives.
items.markingKey: e.g. send letters with a pre-booked appointment time (default), reminders by text, or make the vaccination point easy to reach; this uses inertia and salience rather than incentives.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Nudges are an unacceptable form of manipulation by the government.
items.answer: Nudges are acceptable when transparent, easy to avoid and in line with people's own goals; hidden or self-serving nudges are not.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they work by exploiting biases rather than reasoning; people may not be aware they are being influenced; the government decides what is 'good'. Arguments against: choice is preserved – people can opt out; every choice has an architecture; neutral design is impossible; transparent nudges can be publicly debated. Supported judgement: Nudges are acceptable when transparent, easy to avoid and in line with people's own goals; hidden or self-serving nudges are not.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "default choice".
items.answer: The option that applies automatically unless the person actively chooses something else
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the option that applies automatically unless the person actively chooses something else. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "A tax on sugary drinks is a nudge." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A tax changes economic incentives (the price), so it is not a nudge; a nudge alters choice architecture without significantly changing incentives.
items.markingKey: A tax changes economic incentives (the price), so it is not a nudge; a nudge alters choice architecture without significantly changing incentives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Before a nudge, 50% of 80,000 adults in a region of Spain joined the organ donor register. After introducing an opt-out (presumed consent) system, participation rose to 88%. Calculate the increase in the number of participants.
"Nudges always benefit consumers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Nudges can be used to steer people towards choices that benefit the designer (e.g. firms' pre-ticked add-ons), and governments may misjudge what is in people's interest.
items.markingKey: Nudges can be used to steer people towards choices that benefit the designer (e.g. firms' pre-ticked add-ons), and governments may misjudge what is in people's interest. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the use of choice architecture to reduce household food waste.
items.answer: Possible nudges: smaller plates in canteens, clearer date labels, default smaller portions, feedback on waste; advantages: cheap, preserve choice; disadvantages: small effects, hard to measure, may need taxes/charges; examples from trials (e.g. removing trays in university canteens).
items.markingKey: Possible nudges: smaller plates in canteens, clearer date labels, default smaller portions, feedback on waste; advantages: cheap, preserve choice; disadvantages: small effects, hard to measure, may need taxes/charges; examples from trials (e.g. removing trays in university canteens).

items.stem: "Nudges are more effective than taxes in changing consumer behaviour." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Nudges work well where inertia is the main problem, but for harmful goods with strong habits, price incentives or regulation are usually more effective; the best policy often combines them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: low cost, preserve freedom; large effects when defaults are used (pensions, organ donation); avoid regressive effects of taxes. Arguments against: effects can be small or short-lived for many nudges; taxes give strong, reliable incentives and raise revenue (sugar tax reformulation); nudges can be seen as manipulative. Supported judgement: Nudges work well where inertia is the main problem, but for harmful goods with strong habits, price incentives or regulation are usually more effective; the best policy often combines them. items.stem: Define the term "profit maximisation".
items.answer: The business objective of producing the output at which the difference between total revenue and total cost is greatest (where MC = MR)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the business objective of producing the output at which the difference between total revenue and total cost is greatest (where MC = MR). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a firm might pursue corporate social responsibility even if it raises costs.
items.answer: CSR can improve brand image and customer loyalty, attract talented workers and ethical investors, avoid regulation and reputational damage, so it may raise long-run profits as well as reflecting owners' values.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: CSR can improve brand image and customer loyalty, attract talented workers and ethical investors, avoid regulation and reputational damage, so it may raise long-run profits as well as reflecting owners' values. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Amazon reported very low or negative profits for many years while expanding rapidly. Identify and explain the business objective this suggests.
items.answer: Growth/market share maximisation: reinvesting revenue in expansion, low prices and infrastructure to dominate the market and gain economies of scale, expecting higher long-run profits.
items.markingKey: Growth/market share maximisation: reinvesting revenue in expansion, low prices and infrastructure to dominate the market and gain economies of scale, expecting higher long-run profits.

items.stem: A student claims that Firms that pursue CSR cannot be profit maximisers. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: CSR and long-run profit maximisation can be compatible: ethical behaviour can increase demand, reduce costs (e.g. energy efficiency) and protect reputation.
items.markingKey: CSR and long-run profit maximisation can be compatible: ethical behaviour can increase demand, reduce costs (e.g. energy efficiency) and protect reputation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Corporate social responsibility is just a marketing strategy."
items.answer: CSR is sometimes mainly marketing, but there is evidence of real changes; its value depends on transparency and verification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: CSR is often used to improve brand image; 'greenwashing' cases (e.g. misleading environmental claims). Arguments against: some firms make genuine changes (Patagonia, B-Corps); investors and regulation increasingly require ESG reporting; CSR can reduce costs and risks. Supported judgement: CSR is sometimes mainly marketing, but there is evidence of real changes; its value depends on transparency and verification.

items.stem: Explain why a new firm may aim for market share rather than profit in its early years.
items.answer: Gaining customers quickly can create network effects, economies of scale and brand loyalty, deterring rivals and allowing higher profits later; e.g. ride-hailing and food delivery platforms ran losses for years.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gaining customers quickly can create network effects, economies of scale and brand loyalty, deterring rivals and allowing higher profits later; e.g. ride-hailing and food delivery platforms ran losses for years. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: CSR and long-run profit maximisation can be compatible: ethical behaviour can increase demand, reduce costs (e.g. energy efficiency) and protect reputation.
items.markingKey: CSR and long-run profit maximisation can be compatible: ethical behaviour can increase demand, reduce costs (e.g. energy efficiency) and protect reputation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Unilever's Sustainable Living Plan (2010-2020), explain how it illustrates corporate social responsibility as a business objective.
items.answer: Unilever set targets to halve its environmental footprint and source agricultural materials sustainably while growing the business. The firm pursued social and environmental goals alongside profit, arguing that sustainable brands grew faster.
items.markingKey: Context (Unilever set targets to halve its environmental footprint and source agricultural materials sustainably while growing the business.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "consistent preferences"?
options: The tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information received (the anchor) when making decisions
The assumption that a consumer's preferences are stable and transitive: if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C
A feature of choice architecture that alters people's behaviour in a predictable way without forbidding options or significantly changing economic incentives
Requiring people to make an explicit decision, for example whether to be an organ donor, rather than relying on a default
items.answer: The assumption that a consumer's preferences are stable and transitive: if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C
items.markingKey: B. "consistent preferences" is the assumption that a consumer's preferences are stable and transitive: if A is preferred to B and B to C, then A is preferred to C.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A branch of economics that uses insights from psychology to explain why people's decisions often deviate from the rational choice model"?
items.answer: behavioural economics
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of behavioural economics.

items.stem: Requiring every driving licence applicant to state whether they wish to be an organ donor is an example of what?
items.answer: Mandated choice
items.markingKey: Mandated choice. People must actively make a decision.

items.stem: Explain the difference between profit maximisation and satisficing.
items.answer: Profit maximisation aims for the greatest possible profit (MC = MR); satisficing aims for a satisfactory profit that keeps stakeholders content.
items.markingKey: Profit maximisation aims for the greatest possible profit (MC = MR); satisficing aims for a satisfactory profit that keeps stakeholders content. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between price and utility.
items.answer: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gains from a good; price is what must be paid for it. A rational consumer compares the two at the margin.
items.markingKey: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gains from a good; price is what must be paid for it. A rational consumer compares the two at the margin. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that Behavioural economics shows that people are irrational and their behaviour cannot be predicted. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Behavioural economics shows that deviations from rational choice are systematic and predictable (e.g. anchoring, present bias), which is why they can be used in policy design.
items.markingKey: Behavioural economics shows that deviations from rational choice are systematic and predictable (e.g. anchoring, present bias), which is why they can be used in policy design. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why governments might prefer nudges to taxes or bans.
items.answer: Nudges are cheap, preserve freedom of choice, avoid the political unpopularity of taxes and bans and can be tested quickly with trials.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nudges are cheap, preserve freedom of choice, avoid the political unpopularity of taxes and bans and can be tested quickly with trials. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Profit maximisation means charging the highest possible price." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Profit maximisation means choosing the output where MC = MR; a very high price may reduce quantity so much that profit falls.
items.markingKey: Profit maximisation means choosing the output where MC = MR; a very high price may reduce quantity so much that profit falls. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Utility is the satisfaction a consumer gains from a good; price is what must be paid for it. A rational consumer compares the two at the margin.

items.stem: With reference to gym memberships in the US, explain how it illustrates bounded self-control.
items.answer: Research by DellaVigna and Malmendier found that members on monthly contracts paid more per visit than if they had paid per visit, because they attended less than expected. Consumers over-estimate their future self-control and choose contracts that do not maximise their utility.
items.markingKey: Context (Research by DellaVigna and Malmendier found that members on monthly contracts paid more per visit than if they had paid per visit, because they attended less than expected.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: A student claims that a tax on sugary drinks is a nudge. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A tax changes economic incentives (the price), so it is not a nudge; a nudge alters choice architecture without significantly changing incentives.
items.markingKey: A tax changes economic incentives (the price), so it is not a nudge; a nudge alters choice architecture without significantly changing incentives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Unilever's Sustainable Living Plan (2010-2020) and explain what it reveals about corporate social responsibility as a business objective.
items.answer: Unilever set targets to halve its environmental footprint and source agricultural materials sustainably while growing the business. The firm pursued social and environmental goals alongside profit, arguing that sustainable brands grew faster.
items.markingKey: Context (Unilever set targets to halve its environmental footprint and source agricultural materials sustainably while growing the business.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The firm pursued social and environmental goals alongside profit, arguing that sustainable brands grew faster. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to corporate social responsibility as a business objective.

items.stem: Mateo chooses a phone plan without reading all 15 plans available because comparing them would take hours. Explain which assumption of rational consumer choice this challenges.
items.answer: Perfect information (and the ability to process it): information is costly to obtain, so he makes a satisfactory rather than optimal choice – bounded rationality.
items.markingKey: Perfect information (and the ability to process it): information is costly to obtain, so he makes a satisfactory rather than optimal choice – bounded rationality.

items.stem: A student claims that Buying a gym membership and never going is an example of bounded selfishness. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It is an example of bounded self-control (and over-optimism): people overestimate their future willpower. Bounded selfishness concerns concern for others.
items.markingKey: It is an example of bounded self-control (and over-optimism): people overestimate their future willpower. Bounded selfishness concerns concern for others. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to automatic enrolment in UK workplace pensions from 2012, explain how it illustrates default choices as a nudge.
items.answer: Employers had to enrol eligible workers automatically, who could opt out; participation in private-sector schemes rose from around 42% in 2012 to over 85% by 2019. Workers' inertia now worked in favour of saving, raising participation dramatically without compulsion.
items.markingKey: Context (Employers had to enrol eligible workers automatically, who could opt out; participation in private-sector schemes rose from around 42% in 2012 to over 85% by 2019.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Workers' inertia now worked in favour of saving, raising participation dramatically without compulsion. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to default choices as a nudge.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Profit maximisation means charging the highest possible price." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Profit maximisation means choosing the output where MC = MR; a very high price may reduce quantity so much that profit falls.
items.markingKey: Profit maximisation means choosing the output where MC = MR; a very high price may reduce quantity so much that profit falls. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the three main assumptions of rational consumer choice and, for each, give one example of real-world behaviour that challenges it.
items.answer: Consistent preferences – preference reversals or framing effects; perfect information – complex insurance or energy tariffs; utility maximisation – satisficing, impulse buying, choosing default options. Each explained with a specific example.
items.markingKey: Consistent preferences – preference reversals or framing effects; perfect information – complex insurance or energy tariffs; utility maximisation – satisficing, impulse buying, choosing default options. Each explained with a specific example.

items.stem: Explain, with examples, how firms might use their knowledge of consumer biases to increase sales, and discuss whether governments should regulate such practices.
items.answer: Anchoring (reference prices), framing ('limited time offer'), default add-ons, drip pricing; regulation arguments: protecting consumers from exploitation, information asymmetry; against: paternalism, consumer freedom, costs; examples: EU rules on pre-ticked boxes, 'fake' discounts.
items.markingKey: Anchoring (reference prices), framing ('limited time offer'), default add-ons, drip pricing; regulation arguments: protecting consumers from exploitation, information asymmetry; against: paternalism, consumer freedom, costs; examples: EU rules on pre-ticked boxes, 'fake' discounts.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Nudges are more effective than taxes in changing consumer behaviour?
items.answer: Nudges work well where inertia is the main problem, but for harmful goods with strong habits, price incentives or regulation are usually more effective; the best policy often combines them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: low cost, preserve freedom; large effects when defaults are used (pensions, organ donation); avoid regressive effects of taxes. Arguments against: effects can be small or short-lived for many nudges; taxes give strong, reliable incentives and raise revenue (sugar tax reformulation); nudges can be seen as manipulative. Supported judgement: Nudges work well where inertia is the main problem, but for harmful goods with strong habits, price incentives or regulation are usually more effective; the best policy often combines them. items.stem: "Profit maximisation is the most realistic assumption about the objectives of firms." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Profit is central in the long run, but in practice firms pursue a mix of objectives, so profit maximisation is a useful simplification rather than a complete description.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: firms that fail to make profits do not survive; shareholders pressure managers for returns; explains many pricing and output decisions. Arguments against: separation of ownership and control; CSR, market share and growth goals are common; firms lack the information to find MC = MR exactly (satisficing). Supported judgement: Profit is central in the long run, but in practice firms pursue a mix of objectives, so profit maximisation is a useful simplification rather than a complete description. items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of rational consumer choice?
options: Consumers are influenced by how choices are framed
items.answer: Consumers are influenced by how choices are framed
items.markingKey: D. Framing effects are a finding of behavioural economics that challenges rational choice.

items.stem: Define the term "behavioural economics".
items.answer: A branch of economics that uses insights from psychology to explain why people's decisions often deviate from the rational choice model
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a branch of economics that uses insights from psychology to explain why people's decisions often deviate from the rational choice model. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "default choice"?
options: The assumption that consumers make choices that maximise their utility, given their preferences, incomes and prices
The business objective of producing the output at which the difference between total revenue and total cost is greatest (where MC = MR)
Requiring people to make an explicit decision, for example whether to be an organ donor, rather than relying on a default
The option that applies automatically unless the person actively chooses something else
items.answer: The option that applies automatically unless the person actively chooses something else
items.markingKey: D. "default choice" is the option that applies automatically unless the person actively chooses something else.

items.stem: Distinguish between satisficing and profit maximisation.
items.answer: Profit maximisation aims for the greatest possible profit (MC = MR); satisficing aims for a satisfactory profit that keeps stakeholders content.
items.markingKey: Profit maximisation aims for the greatest possible profit (MC = MR); satisficing aims for a satisfactory profit that keeps stakeholders content. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Rational consumers always buy the cheapest product." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rational consumers maximise utility given their budget, which may mean paying more for a product that gives more satisfaction.
items.markingKey: Rational consumers maximise utility given their budget, which may mean paying more for a product that gives more satisfaction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Behavioural economics shows that people are irrational and their behaviour cannot be predicted." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Behavioural economics shows that deviations from rational choice are systematic and predictable (e.g. anchoring, present bias), which is why they can be used in policy design.
items.markingKey: Behavioural economics shows that deviations from rational choice are systematic and predictable (e.g. anchoring, present bias), which is why they can be used in policy design. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a default choice and a mandated choice.
items.answer: A default applies automatically unless a person opts out; mandated choice requires everyone to make an active decision with no pre-set option.
items.markingKey: A default applies automatically unless a person opts out; mandated choice requires everyone to make an active decision with no pre-set option. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how a nudge such as automatic pension enrolment can increase saving, using the idea of bounded self-control, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: market for retirement saving; without the nudge, present bias means the quantity saved (Q1, where the perceived marginal benefit curve meets the cost) is below the level Q* consistent with workers' long-run interests (true marginal benefit). Auto-enrolment shifts the effective demand for saving towards the true MB curve, increasing quantity from Q1 towards Q*.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: market for retirement saving; without the nudge, present bias means the quantity saved (Q1, where the perceived marginal benefit curve meets the cost) is below the level Q* consistent with workers' long-run interests (true marginal benefit). Auto-enrolment shifts the effective demand for saving towards the true MB curve, increasing quantity from Q1 towards Q*. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the difference between the output chosen by a profit-maximising firm and by a revenue-maximising firm.
items.answer: Diagram: firm with downward-sloping AR (demand) and MR, and MC and AC curves. Profit maximisation at Qπ where MC = MR, price from AR. Revenue maximisation at QR where MR = 0, a higher output and lower price; profit is lower than at Qπ but the firm gains sales and market share.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: firm with downward-sloping AR (demand) and MR, and MC and AC curves. Profit maximisation at Qπ where MC = MR, price from AR. Revenue maximisation at QR where MR = 0, a higher output and lower price; profit is lower than at Qπ but the firm gains sales and market share. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Using the large number of mobile phone and energy tariffs in many countries as an example, explain the limits of the perfect information assumption.
items.answer: Studies by regulators such as the UK's Ofgem found that many consumers stayed on expensive default tariffs rather than switching. Complex tariffs make full comparison difficult, so consumers do not maximise utility as the rational model predicts.
items.markingKey: Context (Studies by regulators such as the UK's Ofgem found that many consumers stayed on expensive default tariffs rather than switching.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Complex tariffs make full comparison difficult, so consumers do not maximise utility as the rational model predicts. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of the perfect information assumption.

items.stem: A university canteen puts water rather than soft drinks in the most visible fridge by the checkout. Identify the type of nudge and explain how it works.
items.answer: Choice architecture (salience/placement): the healthier option is more prominent, so more students choose it without any ban or price change.
items.markingKey: Choice architecture (salience/placement): the healthier option is more prominent, so more students choose it without any ban or price change.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Consumers generally act in their own best interests.
items.answer: Consumers often act in their own interest, but systematic biases and information problems mean they sometimes do not, which justifies some policy responses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: people know their own preferences best; markets respond to consumer choices. Arguments against: biases such as present bias and anchoring cause systematic mistakes; imperfect information and complexity (pensions, insurance); addiction and habits. Supported judgement: Consumers often act in their own interest, but systematic biases and information problems mean they sometimes do not, which justifies some policy responses.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that behavioural economics provides a more accurate explanation of consumer behaviour than traditional rational choice theory.
items.answer: Behavioural economics improves the explanation of many individual decisions, but rational choice remains a useful benchmark for aggregate market behaviour.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: evidence of anchoring, framing, present bias and social norms; explains under-saving, over-eating and inertia; has produced successful policies (auto-enrolment). Arguments against: many findings come from laboratory experiments and may not generalise; rational choice predicts aggregate market responses well; biases vary across people and contexts and some studies fail to replicate. Judgement: Behavioural economics improves the explanation of many individual decisions, but rational choice remains a useful benchmark for aggregate market behaviour. items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that nudges are an unacceptable form of manipulation by the government.
items.answer: Nudges are acceptable when transparent, easy to avoid and in line with people's own goals; hidden or self-serving nudges are not.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they work by exploiting biases rather than reasoning; people may not be aware they are being influenced; the government decides what is 'good'. Arguments against: choice is preserved – people can opt out; every choice has an architecture; neutral design is impossible; transparent nudges can be publicly debated. Judgement: Nudges are acceptable when transparent, easy to avoid and in line with people's own goals; hidden or self-serving nudges are not. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that corporate social responsibility is just a marketing strategy.
items.answer: CSR is sometimes mainly marketing, but there is evidence of real changes; its value depends on transparency and verification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: CSR is often used to improve brand image; 'greenwashing' cases (e.g. misleading environmental claims). Arguments against: some firms make genuine changes (Patagonia, B-Corps); investors and regulation increasingly require ESG reporting; CSR can reduce costs and risks.
